title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 cleaned smart-meter readings for 2024 shows total consumption of 1,207,700 kWh across 12 meters. Industrial sites dominate usage, accounting for over 82% of all energy consumed. Consumption peaked in Q4 and Q1, with a modest 4.7% increase from H1 to H2. Peak and off-peak tariffs are nearly balanced. A moderate negative correlation between temperature and commercial energy use suggests cooling-driven demand is not the primary commercial driver.

key_findings.statement: Across all 1,428 readings in the cleaned dataset, total electricity consumption reached 1,207,700 kWh, yielding a mean of approximately 845.7 kWh per reading.

Industrial buildings consumed the most energy at 995,362 kWh (82.4% of total), followed by Commercial at 196,367 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,971 kWh (1.3%). Industrial usage is approximately 5.1 times that of Commercial.

Quarterly consumption shows a U-shaped pattern: Q4 was highest at 352,882 kWh, followed by Q1 (319,678 kWh), Q2 (270,277 kWh), and Q3 (264,863 kWh) — the lowest quarter. This suggests elevated demand in colder months.
Second-half consumption (617,745 kWh) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955 kWh) by approximately 27,790 kWh, representing an increase of 4.7% from H1 to H2.

On hot days (temperature ≥ 25 °C), 19 commercial readings were recorded with a mean consumption of 415.3 kWh per reading, which is below the overall dataset mean of 845.7 kWh, suggesting commercial sites do not exhibit unusually high load on hot days.

The distribution of consumption is right-skewed: the median is 406.8 kWh while the standard deviation is 913.4 kWh, indicating a long upper tail driven by high-use industrial meters. The mean recorded temperature was 11.6 °C, with 62 readings missing temperature data. For commercial sites, the Pearson correlation between temperature and energy use is −0.64, a moderate negative relationship suggesting commercial consumption tends to be higher in cooler conditions.

Peak-tariff consumption (599,624 kWh, 49.7% of total) and off-peak consumption (608,076 kWh, 50.3%) are nearly equal, indicating no strong tariff-driven load shift. The dataset covers 12 distinct meters; the highest-consuming single meter recorded 252,241 kWh — about 20.9% of total consumption.

limitations: 62 readings have missing temperature data, which may introduce bias into temperature-based analyses, particularly the commercial correlation estimate.
Only 19 hot-day commercial readings (temperature ≥ 25 °C) were available, making the hot-day commercial mean statistically fragile and potentially unrepresentative.
With only 12 distinct meters, the dataset is small; results — especially the single-meter maximum — may not generalise to the broader meter population.
The analysis uses calendar quarters and half-years as fixed boundaries; any seasonal effects that straddle these boundaries may be partially obscured.
Correlation between temperature and commercial energy use is observational; no causal inference can be drawn without controlling for other variables such as occupancy or production schedules.
conclusion: Industrial sites overwhelmingly drive total consumption, and demand is highest in the colder bookend quarters (Q4 and Q1). The modest 4.7% H2 increase and near-equal peak/off-peak split suggest stable load patterns with limited tariff arbitrage. Attention should focus on the single highest-use meter (252,241 kWh) and on improving temperature data completeness to strengthen future seasonal analyses.
